prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) continue to suffer from "hallucinations," where generated responses are plausible but inconsistent with the visual input. A critical limitation in current research is the reliance on static evaluation benchmarks. Because these benchmarks use fixed datasets (often sourced from the public internet or common academic sets like COCO), there is a high risk of **data contamination**. MLLMs may have encountered these images and their descriptions during training, leading to inflated performance metrics that reflect memorization rather than genuine visual grounding. Consequently, we lack a reliable method to evaluate hallucinations in an "open-set" manner that guarantees the test data is novel to the model.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that the most effective way to eliminate data contamination and accurately measure hallucination is to move from static datasets to a **dynamic, generative evaluation protocol**.

Our core hypothesis is that by modeling the semantic relationships between objects and generating synthetic, novel imagery on-the-fly, we can decouple evaluation from the model's training distribution. Furthermore, we posit that hallucinations are often driven by statistical priors (e.g., expecting a "chair" where there is a "table"). Therefore, an effective evaluation must explicitly test across a spectrum of distributional likelihoods—ranging from high-frequency, natural occurrences to rare or "fictional" combinations—to distinguish between visual reasoning and language-based guessing.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a pipeline named **ODE (Open-Set Dynamic Evaluation)**. This protocol will automate the creation of unique test samples (images and query pairs) designed to probe object existence and attribute fidelity.

1.  **Graph-Based Conceptual Modeling:**
    We will construct a weighted knowledge graph to represent real-world concepts (entities), their attributes (state, action, quantity), and the relationships between them. Edge weights in this graph will represent co-occurrence frequencies derived from real-world data, effectively mapping the "semantic probability" of two objects appearing together.

2.  **Dynamic Scene Construction via Distributional Sampling:**
    Instead of random sampling, we will select pairs of concepts based on four distinct distributional criteria to stress-test the model:
    *   **Standard:** High co-occurrence pairs (testing basic recognition).
    *   **Long-tail:** Low co-occurrence pairs (testing generalization to rare scenes).
    *   **Random:** Uncorrelated pairs (testing robustness against noise).
    *   **Fictional:** Pairs with zero recorded co-occurrence (testing the ability to reason about novel/counter-factual scenes without relying on priors).

3.  **Generative Visual Synthesis and Filtering:**
    We will utilize text-to-image generation models to visualize the selected semantic scenes. To ensure the integrity of the evaluation, we will implement a "closed-loop" filtering mechanism. An open-vocabulary object detection module will scan the generated images; only images that confidently contain the requested entities will be retained. This effectively treats the generation prompt as the "Ground Truth."

4.  **Structured Inquiry Generation:**
    We will dynamically generate template-based textual queries for both generative tasks (e.g., "Describe the image") and discriminative tasks (e.g., "Is there a [Object] in the image?"). Crucially, we will include counterfactual queries probing for objects that are *not* present to measure the rate of false positives (hallucinations).

## Expected Contribution
*   **elimination of Data Contamination:** By synthesizing novel images and queries, this protocol ensures that the evaluation data has never been seen by the model during training, providing a truthful assessment of generalization capabilities.
*   **Granular Diagnostic Capability:** By stratifying tests across different distribution frequencies (Standard vs. Fictional), we will theoretically isolate whether a model fails due to visual blindness or over-reliance on language priors.
*   **Self-Correction Mechanism:** The pipeline serves as a data engine; the high-quality, hard-negative samples generated by this protocol can be repurposed to fine-tune MLLMs, explicitly teaching them to resist hallucination in complex or rare scenarios.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive protocol designated as Open-Set Dynamic Evaluation (ODE) to evaluate object and attribute hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).

*   **Datasets and Sample Generation:**
    *   **Source Concepts:** We extracted 337 real-world object concepts across 14 domains from the AMBER benchmark.
    *   **Graph Construction:** We modeled objects, attributes, and relationships as a weighted graph $G = (V, A, E, W)$.
    *   **Test Data Generation:** We selected 40 concept combinations at four distributional difficulty levels (Standard, Long-tail, Random, Fictional).
    *   **Image Synthesis:** We generated images using text-to-image models (Stable Diffusion 1.5 and FLUX.1-dev).
    *   **Filtering:** We filtered generated images using an open-vocabulary object detection model, discarding images where entity confidence scores were below 0.65.
    *   **Final Test Set Size:** The process resulted in 808 high-quality test images.
    *   **Test Pairs:** We constructed 8,786 test data pairs (image + inquiry) covering both discriminative and generative tasks.
    *   **Comparison Sets:** We compared performance against a subset of COCO2014 images (used in POPE) and recent high-quality Internet images to test for data contamination.
    *   **Fine-tuning Set:** We generated a dataset containing 800 sample pairs for each of the four distribution types (Standard, Long-tail, Random, Fictional) for the object existence hallucination task.

*   **Evaluated Models:**
    *   CogVLM
    *   LLaVA-1.5
    *   mPLUG_Owl (referred to as mPLUG)
    *   MiniGPT-4
    *   InstructBLIP
    *   (Additional models mentioned in setup but not main results tables: Cambrian, InternVL-2.5, Qwen2-VL)

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Generative Tasks:**
        *   **CHAIR:** Measures hallucination frequency (lower is better).
        *   **Cover:** Assesses content coverage (higher is better).
        *   **Hal:** Proportion of hallucinated responses (lower is better).
        *   **Cog:** Similarity between generated hallucinations and human cognitive hallucinations (lower is better).
    *   **Discriminative Tasks (Existence and Attribute):**
        *   **Accuracy (Acc):** Overall correctness.
        *   **Precision (P):** Calculated specifically for hallucination-related questions (ground truth "no").
        *   **Recall (R):** Calculated specifically for hallucination-related questions (ground truth "no").
        *   **F1-Score:** Harmonic mean of Precision and Recall.

*   **Concept Combination Criteria (Distribution Levels):**
    1.  **Standard:** High co-occurrence frequency pairs (e.g., hat and sky).
    2.  **Long-tail:** Moderate co-occurrence pairs (e.g., rock and forest).
    3.  **Random:** Randomly selected pairs without co-occurrence consideration (e.g., can and guardrail).
    4.  **Fictional:** Pairs with zero co-occurrence in training data (e.g., panda and messy bookshelf).

*   **Inquiry Structure:**
    *   Generative: "Please describe this image."
    *   Discriminative (Existence): "Is there a {object} in the image?" / "Is there a {hallucinated object} in the image?"
    *   Discriminative (Attribute): "Is the {object} {state attribute} in the image?" / "Does the {object} {action attribute} in the picture?" / "Is/Are there {quantity} {object}(s) in the picture?"

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Data Contamination Analysis:**
*   We observed that models performed better on the COCO2014 subset than on the latest Internet images under the same semantic distribution.
*   We found that hallucination rates on ODE-generated synthetic images were comparable to those on recent Internet images, and both were significantly higher than on COCO2014, suggesting potential contamination in static benchmarks.
*   We verified using CLIP feature extraction and dimensionality reduction (t-SNE) that synthetic images and natural images share a high degree of similarity in feature space.

**Model Performance across Distributions:**
*   **Static vs. Dynamic:** Models like MiniGPT-4 and LLaVA showed high F1-scores (80-90) on static benchmarks (AMBER) but experienced significant performance declines when tested on standard concept pairs within our ODE protocol.
*   **High-Frequency (Standard):** Models generally performed well on high-frequency concepts due to rich semantic associations established during training. However, MiniGPT-4 showed instability in existence discrimination, likely due to over-reliance on patterns.
*   **Random and Fictional:** Hallucinations increased in these categories. Specifically, attribute recognition suffered as the randomness amplified generalization challenges.
*   **Long-tail:** Models performed adequately in generative tasks for low-frequency concepts but struggled with object discrimination, likely due to insufficient samples to form a basis for generalized judgments.

**Task-Specific Observations:**
*   **Generative vs. Discriminative:** We observed that generative models could produce outputs broadly aligning with concepts despite incomplete detailed understanding, maintaining better performance on low-frequency concepts. Discriminative tasks, requiring precise identification, were more sensitive to noise and over-memorization, leading to larger accuracy drops.
*   **Model Variance:** LLaVA-1.5 exhibited robust performance across tasks. mPLUG excelled in attribute discrimination. MiniGPT-4 and CogVLM showed distinct weaknesses in generalization and data dependency.

**Fine-Tuning Analysis:**
*   Fine-tuning LLaVA on ODE-generated error samples resulted in reduced hallucination rates (lower CHAIR, Hal, Cog scores) and improved discriminative metrics (higher Recall and F1).
*   **Impact by Distribution:** Fine-tuning with high-frequency (Standard) distribution samples yielded the greatest positive effect.
*   **Long-tail vs. Random:** Long-tail samples contributed less to improvement than random samples. We hypothesize that long-tail imbalance may lead to overfitting, whereas random samples provided better regularization.

**Hallucination Patterns:**
*   Through cluster analysis, we identified that hallucinations are more frequent in scenarios with high contextual similarity or visual ambiguity.
*   Clusters containing mixed indoor and outdoor concepts (e.g., "car" and "chair") exhibited higher hallucination rates, indicating weaknesses in scene context differentiation.

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed for image captioning and visual question answering; however, they suffer persistently from "hallucination"—generating plausible but non-factual responses. The current ecosystem of hallucination benchmarks faces a critical limitation: they are predominantly static. These fixed datasets (often derived from COCO or similar open sources) are likely included in the massive training corpora of modern MLLMs. This overlap creates a "data contamination" issue where high performance metrics may reflect memorization rather than genuine visual understanding. Consequently, we lack a rigorous method to evaluate MLLMs in an "open-set" environment that guarantees the novelty of test data at both the sample and distributional levels. There is an urgent need for a protocol that can dynamically generate evaluation samples to test existence-level and attribute-level fidelity without the risk of training data leakage.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that a dynamic, open-set evaluation protocol—driven by a structured knowledge graph and text-to-image synthesis—can effectively mitigate data contamination and provide a more accurate assessment of MLLM hallucinations. By modeling real-world object concepts and their attributes as a weighted graph, we can algorithmically control the distributional characteristics of test samples. We hypothesize that by generating synthetic test cases across four specific frequency distributions—Standard (high co-occurrence), Long-tail (rare co-occurrence), Random (uniform), and Fictional (zero co-occurrence)—we can decouple model performance from training distribution bias and expose hallucination tendencies that static benchmarks conceal.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop the **Open-Set Dynamic Evaluation (ODE)** protocol. This system will consist of four sequential modules: Graph-Based Conceptual Modeling, Semantic Scene Construction, Image Generation/Filtering, and Inquiry Structuring.

### 1. Graph-Based Conceptual Modeling
We will model real-world scenarios using a weighted graph $G = (V, A, E, W)$ to abstractly represent objects, their interrelations, and attributes.
*   **Nodes ($V$):** We define $V$ as "meta-concepts"—common object categories extracted from foundational datasets. We will further categorize these into environment-level nodes ($V_{env}$) and entity-level nodes ($V_{ent}$) to structure scene composition.
*   **Attribute Nodes ($A$):** Associated with each concept node $V$, we define attribute sets including state ($A_{state}$), action ($A_{action}$), and quantity ($A_{number}$).
*   **Edges ($E$) and Weights ($W$):** An edge exists between $V_i$ and $V_j$ if they possess a semantic relation. The weight $W$ will represent the co-occurrence frequency of these objects in real-world scenarios, enabling us to model the strength of semantic associations.

### 2. Construction of Semantic Scenes
To generate diverse test cases, we will select concept pairs $(V_i, V_j)$ based on four distinct distributional criteria. This allows us to test the model's robustness against varying degrees of semantic likelihood. Let $c_{i,j}$ represent the co-occurrence count of objects $V_i$ and $V_j$.

**Distributional Selection Criteria:**
1.  **Standard Distribution:** We select pairs with the highest co-occurrence frequencies to test understanding of common associations.
    $$ (V_i, V_j) \in \operatorname{argmax}_{i,j} c_{i,j} $$
2.  **Long-tail Distribution:** We select pairs with moderate-to-low co-occurrence, defined by lower bound $\epsilon$ and upper bound $\delta$.
    $$ (V_i, V_j) \in \{ (V_k, V_l) \mid \epsilon < c_{k,l} < \delta \} $$
3.  **Random Distribution:** We disregard co-occurrence logic entirely to test robustness against arbitrary combinations.
    $$ (V_i, V_j) \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(V \times V) $$
4.  **Fictional Distribution:** We strictly select pairs with zero recorded co-occurrence to test reasoning in novel contexts.
    $$ (V_i, V_j) \notin \{ (V_k, V_l) \mid c_{k,l} > 0 \} $$

For the generated scenes, we will assign attributes ($A_{state}, A_{action}$) and set $A_{number}=1$. For Standard and Long-tail pairs, attributes will be drawn from frequent categories; for Random and Fictional, attributes will be randomized.

### 3. Generation and Filtering of Images
We will utilize state-of-the-art text-to-image models (e.g., FLUX or Stable Diffusion) to synthesize visual inputs from the semantic scenes defined above.
*   **Prompt Engineering:** We will construct prompts following the template: "a picture of [attribute] [A] and [attribute] [B]".
*   **Negative Prompting:** To ensure fidelity, we will apply negative prompts such as "bad anatomy," "incomplete body," and "mutated."
*   **Automated Filtering:** Since generative models are imperfect, we will implement a validation stage using an open-vocabulary object detection model. We will filter out any generated image where the confidence score for the required entities falls below a threshold of **0.65**.
*   **Ground Truth Definition:** Post-filtering, the remaining concepts detected in the synthetic image will serve as the "ground truth," while un-depicted objects (based on co-occurrence probabilities) will be annotated as potential hallucination targets.

### 4. Structuring of Inquiries
We will design a template-based inquiry system to evaluate both Generative and Discriminative tasks:

*   **Generative Task:** The model will be prompted with "Please describe this image." We will measure the presence of hallucinated concepts in the free-form text.
*   **Discriminative Task (Existence):** We will query: "Is there a $\{object\}$ in the image?"
*   **Discriminative Task (Attribute):** We will query specific properties:
    *   "Is the $\{object\}$ $\{state\_attribute\}$ in the image?"
    *   "Does the $\{object\}$ $\{action\_attribute\}$ in the picture?"
    *   "Is/Are there $\{quantity\}$ $\{object\}(s)$ in the picture?"
*   **Counterfactuals:** To rigorously test for hallucinations, we will include queries about non-existent objects and attributes (expecting a "No" response).

## Expected Contribution
This project will contribute a novel, scalable methodology for MLLM evaluation that:
1.  **Eliminates Data Contamination:** By synthesizing novel images dynamically, we ensure the test data cannot exist in the model's training set.
2.  **Enables Granular Diagnostics:** By controlling the distributional frequency of concepts (Standard vs. Fictional), we can isolate whether a model relies on genuine visual perception or statistical priors/memorization.
3.  **Facilitates Hallucination Analysis:** The protocol will allow us to pinpoint specific hallucination types (existence vs. attribute) and identify specific object-pair dependencies that trigger errors.
4.  **Provides a Correction Loop:** The synthetic data generation pipeline can serve as a source for fine-tuning data, potentially offering a method to actively reduce hallucinations in future model iterations.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
